Master's examination · Artificial Intelligence

Data-based Numerical Simulation of Buoyant Jet Flow

What a recurrence replay loses when the scalar drives the flow, and how much of it can be repaired

MSc thesis defense

Supervisor: Prof. Stefan Pirker · Department of Particulate Flow Modelling

JKUJohannes Kepler University Linz
Good morning. Thank you for being here. My thesis is about recurrence CFD, a data-based way to simulate long industrial processes cheaply. The question is simple: the method was built for a scalar that is only carried by the flow. What happens when the scalar drives the flow itself, like temperature in a buoyant jet? And how much of what is lost can we repair without solving the flow again? I will answer this in three claims and one open point.
The method

Simulate the flow once. Replay it many times.

A full CFD run records how the fluid moves, frame by frame, as cell-to-cell maps.

The replay applies these maps to the temperature again and again. Momentum and pressure are never solved again.

260×cheaper on average
569 → 1–5minutes per run
Lichtenegger & Pirker 2016 · Pirker et al. 2018 · Thesis Ch. 2, Fig. 2.1
Recurrence CFD, or rCFD, has two stages. First, a normal CFD simulation, the preparation, runs once and records which share of each cell moves to which neighbour, frame by frame. Then the replay applies those stored maps to the temperature. It never solves momentum or pressure again. In my case a reference run takes 569 minutes, a replay between one and five minutes: about 260 times cheaper. From a computer-science view, it trades computation for memory: we cache the expensive part and reuse it.
The question

rCFD was built for a scalar that only rides the flow. Temperature pushes back.

What does the replay lose when the scalar drives the flow, and how much can be repaired without solving the flow again?

Thesis Fig. 1.1
On the left, a passive scalar: a dye that is only stretched by the flow. In the middle, temperature in a buoyant flow: cold plumes from the lid create the motion themselves. On the right, the replay: it moves the temperature with recorded maps, but the feedback from temperature to velocity is cut. So my question is: what does the replay lose in that situation, and how much of it can be repaired without solving the flow again?
The test case

A small tank, a warm jet, and a front that must stay sharp

75×75×15 mm tank1 mm cubic cells warm inflow 333 K for 315 s Re ≈ 99 laminarRi 1.84 buoyancy wins 600 recorded frames

Two lids: adiabatic and cooled (h = 100 W m⁻² K⁻¹).

Reference: ANSYS Fluent, Boussinesq flow. Replay: the rCFD library of the department.

Thesis Ch. 3, Fig. 3.3, Table 3.2
The test case is a closed tank, 75 by 75 by 15 millimetres, on one-millimetre cubes. A warm jet enters at mid-height at 333 kelvin for 315 seconds, then the inflow turns cold and the tank settles. The Reynolds number is about 99, so the flow is laminar, and the Richardson number is 1.84: buoyancy is a bit stronger than inertia, so the jet bends up to the lid and builds a warm layer on top of a sharp front. I studied two lids: an adiabatic one and a cooled one.
Roadmap

Three claims and one open point

1

One knob, two answers

No single mixing constant is best, and the reason is physical.

2

Sharpen safely

A bounded anti-diffusive correction rebuilds the front with no overshoot.

3

The missing cooling

Most of it was a material mismatch, not a transport failure.

4

What remains

A transport defect that only recorded transport can fix.

Here is the plan. First, the standard replay has one free mixing constant, and no single value is best. Second, I add a bounded anti-diffusive correction that rebuilds the front without creating new extremes. Third, under wall cooling most of the missing cooling turns out to be a material mismatch between the two simulations. And fourth, one defect remains, and it is a defect of transport.
Claim 1 · adiabatic lid

One mixing knob, two different best values

The replay adds mixing with a face exchange of strength fsd. Over seven values:

  • Mean temperature is best with little mixing (RMSE 1.07 K).
  • Height of the heat is best near fsd = 0.5.
  • At the largest strength the tank drains 5.08 K too much.
Thesis Ch. 5, Fig. 5.1, Table 5.2
A pure displacement does not mix, so the library adds a face exchange: each step it moves a small share of heat from the warmer to the colder cell. Its strength, f-sd, is the one free constant. I swept seven values. The mean temperature is best with little added mixing. The height of the heat is best around 0.5. The two optima are on opposite sides. And with strong mixing the tank loses up to 5 kelvin too much. Why? The next slide shows it.
Claim 1 · the mechanism

The outlet sits just below the front. A smeared front leaks heat.

A wider front puts warm fluid at the height of the outlet.

+2.7 Kkept in the tank at 315 s
−1.9 Kdrained by the end

With the correction: −0.5 K.

A numerical error at a front becomes an energy error wherever an outlet sits near it.

Thesis Fig. 5.8
The reason is the outlet. It sits just below the front. When the replay smears the front, warm fluid reaches the outlet height and leaves. The running budget shows it: the standard replay first keeps 2.7 kelvin too much while the tank fills, and ends 1.9 kelvin too cold. With my correction it ends at minus 0.5 kelvin. So a purely numerical error at the front becomes an error in the energy budget. That is the first general lesson.
Claim 2 · the idea · live model, not replay data

Anti-diffusion explodes. A local-bounds limiter makes it safe.

Negative diffusion, ν = −0.1

step 0in range

Limited correction, s = 0.25

step 0width 8.8 cells
Δqf = s · min(Qh+, Qc−) · conservative · no new extremum · no clamp needed for s ≤ 1/6
Zalesak 1979 · Boris & Book 1973 · Thesis Sec. 4.2, Fig. 4.1
To undo the smearing, the obvious idea is negative diffusion: move heat from cold to warm. On the left you see why that fails: the problem is ill-posed, the shortest wiggles grow fastest, and a one-millikelvin disturbance leaves the range of the data after about twenty steps. On the right is my correction. Across each face it moves heat up the gradient, but only as much as both cells may still take before they reach the extremes of their neighbourhood. It is conservative, it creates no new extremum, and the front sharpens steadily. This is the idea of flux-corrected transport, applied to a replay.
Claim 2 · direction matters

Act across the front, not along it

Each face gets a weight cos² of its angle to the vertical: the face coefficient of a rank-one diffusion tensor along the front normal.

  • Only the vertical form lowers both errors as the front reaches 5.0 mm.
  • Unweighted, it needs s = 0.9 and leaves a saw-toothed front 3.1 mm too high.
Thesis Sec. 4.2.4, Fig. 5.4
The front is horizontal, so sharpening should act across it, not along it. I weight each face by cos squared of its angle to the vertical, which is the face coefficient of a diffusion tensor along the front normal. In this map every marker is one replay. Only the vertically weighted form brings both errors down while the front reaches the reference width. Without the weight you need a much larger strength, and you get a saw-toothed front. Direction matters more than strength.
Claim 2 · result

The front comes back, and nothing leaves the range of the data

15.7 → 5.3 / 4.5 mmfront width at s = 0.40 / 0.45 · reference 5.0 mm
1.46 → 0.64 Ktrace error
6.05 → 1.39 Kend profile

No end field in any run left the range of the data.

Thesis Ch. 5, Fig. 5.6; Ch. 8 answer to Q2
Here is the result on the adiabatic case. The front goes from 15.7 millimetres to 5.3 and 4.5 at strengths 0.40 and 0.45, bracketing the reference of 5.0. The trace error falls from 1.46 to 0.64 kelvin, the end profile from 6.05 to 1.39. And no field in any run left the range of the data. The profile on the right shows it: without correction the front is wide and too high, with the vertical weight it follows the reference.
Claim 3 · cooled lid

The replay stayed 4.34 K too warm. The budget showed why.

I traced every heat term to the specific heat it was computed with.

reference

"water" with cp of air
1006.43 J kg⁻¹K⁻¹

replay

water
4182 J kg⁻¹K⁻¹

× 4.155same wall power, four times less cooling in the replay
Thesis Ch. 6, Fig. 6.2
Now the cooled lid. The standard replay ended 4.34 kelvin too warm and captured only 37 percent of the cooling. Instead of tuning, I closed the heat budget of both simulations term by term and traced every term to the specific heat it used. The reference material was called water, but it carried the specific heat of air, 1006. The replay was given water, 4182. So the same wall power cooled the replay 4.155 times less. The missing cooling was never missing from the transport.
Claim 3 · result

On one fluid, the replay follows the reference

4.34 → 0.66 Kend error, consistent fluid, declared coefficient
0.06 Kwith the correction at s ≈ 0.55, on 9.62 K of cooling

End profile within 0.41 K; all three zones within 0.2 K.

Thesis Ch. 6, Fig. 6.3; Ch. 8 answer to Q3
On one consistent fluid, with the declared wall coefficient, the replay removes 1542 joules against the imposed 1575 and ends only 0.66 kelvin below the reference. With the correction at its working point it ends 0.06 kelvin off, on a cooling depth of 9.62 kelvin, and the end profile is within 0.41 kelvin. The profile also shows why I report shape and level separately: without correction the replay holds nearly the right heat in the wrong place.
What remains

One defect survives every local repair: it is transport

While the tank fills, the replay separates its layers too slowly. A conservative local rule cannot create missing transport.

A vertical convective flux read from the recording, F = ρcpv(T − T̄), supplies it:

1.66 → 0.26 Kheterogeneity error

Limitation: the flux is tied to the run it was recorded from.

Thesis Sec. 2.8.2, Fig. 6.4
One defect survives. While the tank fills, the replay separates its layers too slowly. No conservative local rule can fix that, because what is missing is transport, not sharpness. So I recorded a vertical convective flux during the preparation and applied its divergence in the replay. The heterogeneity error falls from 1.66 to 0.26 kelvin. The honest limitation: this flux contains the temperature of the run it was recorded from, so it is tied to that case.
The general lesson

A recording belongs to a flow regime, not to a case

After the inflow, the adiabatic flow hardly changes. Under the cooled lid, cold plumes keep renewing it.

A boundary condition switched the regime by itself. In ML words: the new case is out of distribution, and no coefficient recovers a motion the recording never saw.

Thesis Fig. 6.7 · multi-state rCFD: Lichtenegger 2019
The broader lesson. These recurrence plots compare the two recordings. After the inflow the adiabatic flow hardly changes, while under the cooled lid the cold plumes keep renewing the motion. So the cooled lid did not only change a boundary value, it switched the flow into another regime. In machine-learning words, the new case is out of distribution for a database recorded without cooling, and no coefficient can recover a motion that the recording never contained.
Take-home

Three things this tank teaches beyond itself

1

Regime, not case

A recurrence database belongs to a flow regime; a boundary condition can switch the regime by itself.

2

Front → budget

A numerical error at a front becomes an energy error near an outlet; a bounded anti-diffusive correction repairs both.

3

Same fluid, same clock

Two simulations can only be compared on the same fluid and at the same instant.

Next: an implicit exchange so the recorded diffusivity can act · a recorded wall coefficient per cell · multi-state databases.

To close, three lessons that go beyond this tank. First, a recurrence database belongs to a flow regime, and for a non-passive scalar a boundary condition can switch the regime. Second, a numerical error at a front becomes an energy error wherever an outlet is near, and a bounded anti-diffusive correction repairs shape and budget together. Third, compare simulations only on the same fluid and at the same instant: the most expensive errors of this project were exactly these. Next steps would be an implicit exchange, a recorded wall coefficient, and multi-state databases.

Thank you.

Questions are welcome.

The buoyant jet is not recurrent: the replay runs in sequence

Two blocks: filling and settling. No state comes back.

Backup · recorded diffusivity

Why the recorded diffusivity acted like a constant

The exchange is explicit and capped at half a cell per face and step:

Di=DΔtcs2≤0.5

The recorded field asks for Di ≈ 4 in every cell (smallest value 7.2·10⁻⁷ m²/s > 5·10⁻⁷ m²/s). Every face hits the cap, so it behaves like fsd = 0.5: three replays are bit-identical.

Fix: a shorter replay step or an implicit exchange.

Thesis Sec. 2.8.1, Eqs. (2.14)–(2.17)
Backup: the explicit cap of the exchange.
